article.overview: A cryogenic sample storage unit is a containment system that keeps lunar samples at very low temperatures from collection on the Moon until they can be examined in a laboratory. Its main purpose is to preserve water ice and other volatile compounds in their frozen form. NASA-affiliated studies describe temperature requirements for lunar biological and physical-science samples between -100 °C and -153 °C, with a possible lower limit of about -253 °C for geological samples that may contain volatiles from permanently shadowed regions. The concept is defined more by its thermal and containment requirements than by a single standard hardware design. Status as of the research date (2026-11-13): proposed hardware and design requirements. No flown lunar cryogenic sample storage unit was identified in the sources reviewed.
article.description: The payload class covers any sealed container, insulation system, cooling method and interface that can hold a sample at cryogenic temperature. Published concepts combine three elements. First, a sample container that can be sealed and removed or inserted without warming the sample excessively; the NASA/Marshall notional passive concept includes a removable, insulating end cap used to stow or retrieve the sample. Second, a thermal system that is either passive (high-performance insulation plus a consumable coolant such as one based on Joule-Thomson or phase-change cooling) or active (powered cryogenic cooling). Third, interfaces to the spacecraft, lander or ground facility, including power, heat rejection, mass allowance and handling procedures. The NASA/Marshall abstract sets a planning allowance of 700 kg for the container and refrigeration system, with individual lunar samples expected to be below 50 kg. A cryogenic storage unit is distinct from a standard sealed sample container: a sealed container can preserve sample composition against contamination but does not by itself maintain cryogenic temperatures. The Artemis III Science Definition Team report separates these concerns, recommending both hermetically sealed volatile-bearing containers and cryogenic return where the science requires it.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The unit is intended to preserve samples whose scientific value depends on remaining frozen. The Artemis III Science Definition Team report states that cryogenic return increases the scientific yield of samples containing icy and/or volatile components, and recommends that NASA return a subset of samples at temperatures low enough to keep water ice and other low-temperature volatiles solid throughout the journey to Earth-based laboratories. Published rationale identifies several uses. Volatile and ice chemistry: reactions between liquid or gaseous water and other volatile compounds, or between water and minerals at room temperature, can alter chemical, isotopic and textural information, and keeping samples frozen reduces these changes. Cryostratigraphy and texture: the Artemis III report notes that cryogenic transport also preserves textural information in core samples, at both macroscopic and microscopic scales. Polar cold-trap material: Calaway and Allen (2011) state that samples from extremely cold environments, including lunar polar cold traps, could require curation at temperatures as low as 40 K. Technology reuse: the Artemis III report notes that systems able to maintain lunar cryogenic conditions would also be relevant to sample return from Mars, comets and icy outer-planet satellites.
article.operating_principle: Two operating approaches appear in the published work. Passive storage: a passive unit has no power input. Heat is kept out by high-performance insulation and by a shielded sample volume. In the NASA/Marshall notional concept, the sample sits in a vapor-cooled shield, isolated from the outer container by concentric reflective rigid shields and multilayer and/or aerogel insulation; a consumable cooling process absorbs heat that does get through. The abstract states that this approach may be preferred for missions shorter than 30 days because of significant mass savings. Active storage: an active unit uses powered cryogenic cooling. The NASA/Marshall abstract states that active approaches may be necessary to preserve samples for longer periods of time; the published sources do not specify a cryocooler design or its performance for lunar use. Earth-side curation: Calaway and Allen (2011) propose that, on return, the container could be placed in a helium-shroud cryopump vacuum chamber, with cryocontainment maintained through delivery to a cryogenic curation chamber at about 40 K that would include cameras and robotic manipulators. They state that cryogenic curation is feasible with technologies developed for the superconductor industry, but that significant research and development would be needed for lunar volatile samples. The NASA/Marshall analysis estimates that, for an effective emittance of 0.005 through the insulation, heat leak is expected to be below 1.5 W for a 30-litre sample volume relative to a 20 °C environment; the companion abstract also assumes a 0.8 W penalty through the end cap. These are projected analysis values, not measured performance.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar volatiles are scientifically important because they can record the history of water and other compounds on the Moon, and they may be a resource for future exploration. Calaway and Allen (2011) note that lunar polar regolith and rocks have been found to contain small amounts of OH- and/or H2O, which renewed interest in lunar volatile science. The sources reviewed do not indicate that Apollo samples were held cryogenically after return. The Artemis III report cites Apollo 16 sample 66095, known as the 'rusty rock,' as an example of a sample that would have benefited from cryogenic transport and curation; this is an inference from the report's wording rather than a statement about the storage conditions of every Apollo sample. The Artemis III report also recommends lightweight, double-sealed vacuum containers for volatile-bearing samples from the lunar south polar region. Its Finding 6.1.4-4 states that such containment can preserve volatile signatures and prevent gas-exposure hazards in the crew cabin.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, power or temperature specification for a cryogenic sample storage unit. The examples below are a notional passive concept, a return-mission study and a set of published requirements. None of them is a qualified flight design. Values are tied to their source and are not directly comparable.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: For a complete unit, dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The only geometric information is the 30-litre sample volume used in the NASA/Marshall heat-leak analysis. The challenge outcome brief does not give dimensions. No dimension should be treated as a design requirement without checking the original source.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: For a complete unit, mass is not publicly specified. The NASA/Marshall figures apply to the sample (less than 50 kg expected per individual sample) and a 700 kg allowance for the container and refrigeration system. The Georgia Tech study reports up to 6 kg of samples in an abstract-level result. These are planning or study values, not measured masses of hardware.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Passive concepts are described as requiring no electrical power or heat rejection. Active storage requires powered cryogenic cooling, but no power value is published in the sources reviewed. Challenge material asks for low-power or no-power solutions; no numerical limit is verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Published sample-temperature requirements are -100 °C to -153 °C for biological and physical-science samples, and possibly -253 °C for geological samples. The challenge's containment target is at or below -150 °C. Source environment: LRO Diviner observations, as summarised by Calaway and Allen (2011), report polar cold-trap temperatures as low as 38 K and nighttime surface temperatures from 38 K to 90 K; daytime surface temperatures (top 2 cm) are about 180 K to 300 K. These are environmental observations, not storage requirements. Vacuum and thermal isolation: insulation, reflective shields and a sealed volume are needed to limit heat leak; the NASA/Marshall analysis uses a vacuum-insulated concept with a 20 °C external environment. Power and heat rejection: passive concepts are described as requiring neither; active concepts need powered cooling that the sources do not quantify. Handling: samples may need to be handled inside a cold or inert environment after return, and the Artemis III report notes that a room-temperature sealed sample still allows elemental and isotopic analysis once complications are accounted for.
article.limitations: Mass penalty: the Artemis III report says minimising the mass penalty for cryogenic return increases scientific yield because more mass can be allocated to samples rather than hardware. Duration: the NASA/Marshall abstract states that passive approaches are preferred for shorter missions (under 30 days), while longer storage may need active cooling. Cooling-system constraints: search-result summaries of NASA challenge material describe limited space, limited power and cryogenic system longevity as the main problems for lander, Gateway and Orion use; these were not verified against the primary challenge table. Earlier passive assessment: challenge material as summarised in search results notes that passive ice packs were judged unable to maintain the cryogenic temperatures required; not independently verified. Evidence maturity: the reviewed material consists largely of conference papers, a workshop paper, a challenge page and a planning report; none is a flight requirements document.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A cryogenic sample storage unit is a sample-return payload. Its concern is containment, handling, sealing, transfer and the return chain, rather than landing or surface deployment. No compatibility with a named lander, rover, ascent vehicle or spacecraft is asserted.
transportation_process: Collection and sealing: the Artemis III report recommends hermetically sealed, double-sealed vacuum containers for volatile-bearing samples and notes that frozen volatiles should be contained in individually sealed containers. Collection hardware is outside the scope of this payload.

Ascent and transfer: the published sources describe possible routes but do not verify compatibility with any particular lander, ascent vehicle or crew vehicle. The Georgia Tech abstract contrasts a route that stops at the Lunar Gateway, which lengthens transit, with a direct uncrewed return.
Cryogenic transport to curation: the Artemis III report discusses cryogenic transport from the lunar surface to curation facilities as a means of preserving water ice and other volatiles.

Return-chain constraints: the challenge sought a system that could keep samples at -150 °C or colder across the Human Landing System, Gateway and Orion. Whether any current or planned element is compatible with a specific storage unit is not verified.

Earth-side curation: Calaway and Allen (2011) propose placing the container in a helium-shroud cryopump vacuum chamber on return and maintaining cryocontainment through delivery to a cryogenic chamber at about 40 K.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable in the usual surface-deployment sense. The relevant operations are sealing and retrieval of the sample, stowage and removal of the insulating end cap, and transfer into a return or curation system, as described for the NASA/Marshall notional concept.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No flown lunar cryogenic sample storage unit was identified. The Artemis III report cites Apollo 16 sample 66095 as an example of a sample that would have benefited from cryogenic transport and curation.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not verified for any lander, rover, ascent vehicle or crew vehicle. Compatibility would require verified mass, volume, power, thermal, interface and handling specifications for the intended vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The published record shows a sequence of studies and challenges rather than a flown lunar cryogenic storage unit. In 2011, Calaway and Allen presented an analysis of cold and cryogenic curation for lunar volatile samples at the 'A Wet vs. Dry Moon' workshop on 15 June 2011. In 2020, NASA's Artemis III Science Definition Team recommended cryogenic sample return and double-sealed vacuum containers for volatile-bearing samples. In 2020-2021, NASA's Lunar Deep Freeze Challenge sought low-power containment at -150 °C or colder for lunar samples. In 2023, NASA/Marshall published conference material on active and passive storage for low-temperature lunar sample return. In 2026, a Georgia Tech study reported a direct uncrewed return concept for up to 6 kg of samples at 77 K. These sources document planning, requirements and analysis; the reviewed sources did not identify flight-qualified or flown lunar cryogenic sample storage hardware.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flight heritage identified: no flown lunar cryogenic sample storage unit was identified in the sources reviewed. Notional values: the NASA/Marshall heat-leak figure is an analysis result for a notional design, not a measured value. Planning allowances: the 700 kg allowance and the sub-50 kg sample expectation are planning figures, not verified mission limits. Temperature targets differ between sources; the -253 °C figure is described as a possible lower limit for geological samples. Georgia Tech study: the 6 kg, 77 K and direct-return results come from the repository abstract; the full text was not accessible, so assumptions and margins are unverified. Challenge table: the 'Table 1' referred to on the challenge page, which may contain per-vehicle mass, power, volume and duration limits, was not retrieved. Dates and status: the challenge is marked closed and lists a 2021 deadline; current NASA sample-return plans were not confirmed in the research. Search-only information: some statements reported in search-result text (for example, specific per-vehicle durations and a reported mass limit from a challenge listing) could not be verified against a primary document and are not included as facts in the article.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file are cleaned: no query strings or fragments. No image URLs are included because no source-verifiable direct image asset was identified; the article includes no images.

data_quality_notes: No source-verifiable direct image asset for a cryogenic sample storage unit, prototype or flight demonstration was identified in the research. The article and JSON therefore include no images (image registry, overview_images and section arrays are empty). Image search should be repeated if a NASA image-library or Artemis sample-return hardware image is later identified.
No flown lunar cryogenic sample storage unit was identified; all hardware examples are notional, conceptual or requirements-only and are labelled accordingly.
The NASA/Marshall heat-leak figure (below 1.5 W for a 30-litre sample at emittance 0.005) is an analysis result from the presentation and abstract, not a measured value.
The 700 kg container and refrigeration allowance and sub-50 kg sample expectation are planning figures from the NASA/Marshall abstract, not verified mission limits.

The Georgia Tech study (6 kg at 77 K, direct uncrewed return) is based on the repository abstract only. The record page returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool; the authors and date were taken from search-result text and not verified on the record.

The NASA Lunar Deep Freeze Challenge 'Table 1' (per-vehicle mass, power, volume and cold-stowage durations) was not retrieved; the challenge page states only an overall duration of about two weeks. Per-vehicle durations (2, 5 and 6 days for lander, Gateway and Orion) and the 20 cm x 30 cm container assumption and 20 kg mass limit appeared only in search-result text and are excluded from the article as unverified.
The statement that passive ice packs were judged unable to maintain cryogenic temperatures appears only in search-result text summarising challenge material; not verified against a primary document.
The Artemis III report date is given as December 2020 from the document filename and search-result text; the PDF's cover page was not read for the exact day.
The Gomez/Schunk lightning presentation is undated; its date is inferred from the 2023-11 upload path.

Apollo 16 sample 66095 is cited by the Artemis III report as a sample that would have benefited from cryogenic transport; the sources reviewed do not confirm the storage conditions of Apollo samples, so the article does not state them.
The Mitchell 2021 National Academies talk and the 2019 Universe Today report on a lunar ice return white paper were seen only in search-result text and are not cited.

Technical specification audit is incomplete: no dimensions, power or mass values for any complete unit are publicly specified in the sources reviewed; these fields are null or 'not publicly specified'.
Transportation compatibility with any named lander, ascent vehicle, Gateway element or Orion is not verified and is not asserted.
